title: Fulham 0-20 Man City: Inside the longest losing run in English football history
content:
As the snow came down, in the depths of winter in February 2012, there might have been some supporters in the away end at Manchester City who were hoping for an abandonment.

Sergio Aguero had opened the scoring for the most expensively-assembled team in English football. Edin Dzeko also got one, and, in between, Chris Baird turned the ball past Fulham goalkeeper Mark Schwarzer for an own goal. Twice, though, the match had to be delayed because of the lousy conditions.

“The snow was so bad, you couldn’t see the white lines of the pitch,” says Bob Cain, a Fulham fan for over half a century. “I had to watch it on TV, because the weather made it impossible to travel. They stopped the game to clear the lines, and I was praying the referee would abandon it.”

No such luck. The snow got shifted, and it finished 3-0 to City. But what neither set of supporters could have realised was that match would be the start of something extraordinary — good and bad — for both clubs.

Starting with that meeting 14 years ago last week, City have now put together 20 successive wins against Fulham – 17 in the league, two in the FA Cup and one in the League Cup. The aggregate score in those fixtures is 62 goals to 13. Or in terms of league points earned, 51 to zero. It is a record for the English game, going all the way back to the formation of the Football League in 1888.

All of which can make it difficult for someone like Bob, who was in the away end for Fulham’s 3-0 defeat at the Etihad Stadium on Wednesday, clocking up his 558th Fulham game in a row.

Bob hasn’t missed a non-behind-closed-doors first-team match of any sort at Craven Cottage since 1971, the year he started watching Fulham at age 16. His longest run of consecutive home-and-away games attended, domestically, stands at 984 — from 1988 to 2007.

He couldn’t go to that snow-affected game in 2012 because, living in Bexleyheath, Kent, south-east of London, the journey up to Manchester that Saturday was too treacherous. He was also absent for a 2-0 defeat at City in January 2013 because of a family matter, while in the 2020-21 season, the Covid-19 lockdown meant nobody could attend another 2-0 loss for Fulham at the Etihad in the December and a 3-0 one at home three months later.

Bob has been to all the other 16 meetings, though, and, as you can imagine, it has occasionally been a chastening experience.

September 2018 at the Etihad, for example.

“That was one of the worst displays,” recalls Bob, now 70. “We conceded three in the first 47 minutes and, when I got home to watch the highlights on Match of the Day, it was noticeable that half the City fans hadn’t taken their seats at the start of the second half.

“The commentator, Steve Wilson, noted it too. He said, ‘They don’t need to worry about missing a goal. It’s like waiting for a train on the Victoria Line — there will be another one in a minute.’ It stayed at 3-0, and the following Monday I sent him a message on Twitter to ask if he was still on the platform.”

Perhaps it’s just a City thing.

They also have the second-longest winning record in English football, with 16 straight wins against Watford, now of the Championship, including a 6-0 beating in the 2018-19 FA Cup final and an 8-0 at the Etihad in the Premier League early the following season. As for the third-longest winning streak, that is another one with City’s fingerprints all over it — 15 against Bournemouth, from 2015 to 2024.

City manager Pep Guardiola, meanwhile, has won all 17 of his meetings with Fulham counterpart Marco Silva, the longest winning run of his coaching career. Not that this is just a Pep-Marco thing. The 20-match sequence began with Roberto Mancini and then Manuel Pellegrini in City’s dugout, with five other Fulham managers – Martin Jol, Rene Meulensteen, Felix Magath, Slavisa Jokanovic and Scott Parker – sharing the defeats with Silva.

City: WWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWW

Fulham: LLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLL

The strangest thing, perhaps, is that there was once a time when Fulham had a decent record against City, losing only two of the clubs’ first eight encounters in the Premier League era and winning twice themselves. On second thoughts, however, is it really that strange? Maybe not so much, given that all eight of those games came before Abu Dhabi’s 2008 takeover of City changed the landscape of English football.

Silva’s take after their latest defeat was that Fulham had shown “too much respect” for the team that has won eight Premier League titles since this ran began.

At least Bob and his fellow supporters can cling to the memories of overcoming a 2-0 deficit at City as part of what their supporters remember as the ‘Great Escape’, when Fulham won four of their final five matches in the 2007-08 season to save themselves from relegation. At half-time that April day, Roy Hodgson’s team would have been down if results across the division stayed as they were. Instead, the game was turned upside down, culminating in a stoppage-time winner by Diomansy Kamara.

Fulham also won at the Etihad, 3-1, the following year… just never against City since, home or away.

“All these records come to an end eventually,” says Bob, trying to remain upbeat. “We had never won at Everton in our entire history until the lockdown season. This season, we won at Burnley for the first time since 1951. That was my 16th visit to Turf Moor and, until that point, the best I’d seen us get was a few draws.”

And City? The truth is, these records don’t matter too much to them. Guardiola and his team have more important priorities, namely chasing down Arsenal at the top of the Premier League. Twenty in a row? It barely registered in the post-match interviews with Guardiola.

Fulham, meanwhile, must now prepare for Sunday’s trip to Stoke City of the second-tier Championship in the FA Cup. If they get through that tie, no prizes for getting who Bob would like to avoid in the next round.

“I love watching cup draws,” says Bob, “but I always prefer it when we are one of the first names out. You’re looking at the numbers, working out who’s left. Then you hear the dreaded words, ‘And Manchester City will play…’ and you’re thinking, ‘For goodness’ sake, don’t let that next ball be us’.”
